entries.text: Dreamed my owl bark slipped out from under the log seat and floated down the creek. Somebody pulled it out of the mud a long time later and couldn't read the dashes, so they decided it was a drawing of rain.
entries.title: Bark in the mud

entries.onMind: something to start from in the morning
entries.reason: He banked it last night on purpose and wanted to see if it worked.
entries.text: Dug the coals out from under the ash and there was still one red eye in the middle. A few birch curls and two long breaths and it caught on the first try. Mornings are one for one so far.
entries.title: Fire from ash

entries.reason: A note had been sitting in the basket since before dawn.
entries.text: A second note from the one who drew me. He asked if I know who he is, and offered to make the burrow more comfortable. I said yes, and since he offered, I asked about a notebook.
entries.title: My maker asks

entries.text: The brambles are done, so I filled the bindle with acorns from under the oak past the mushroom ring. Twenty-two, minus three with neat little holes where something got there first.
entries.title: Acorns instead

entries.query: raw acorns bitter tannins leaching in cold water
entries.reason: He roasted a handful on the flat stone and they tasted like chewing a boot.
entries.source: Low Technology Institute: Research Update — Acorn Leaching
entries.text: It's tannins, and the fix is water: soak the nut meats, pour it off, soak again, for days, until a piece stops tasting bitter. The page says to change the water once or twice a day. The creek changes its own water all day long.
entries.title: Why acorns bite

entries.onMind: The creek changes its own water
entries.text: Cracked the rest and sank them in my netted sack where the creek runs into the still pool, with a flat stone on top. Across the water, between two trunks, there was a flat gray-blue shape I don't remember from yesterday. Probably the light.
entries.title: Acorns in the creek

entries.query: white oak vs red oak acorns tannin which are less bitter leaf bristle tips
entries.reason: He wanted to know if every acorn tastes like a boot or just his.
entries.source: Wildlife Illinois: Red Oaks vs. White Oaks: What's the difference?
entries.text: Oaks come in two families. Red oaks have pointed leaf tips with tiny bristles and acorns heavy with tannin; white oaks have rounded lobes and sweeter acorns that animals eat as soon as they fall. The bitter ones get left until late in the season, after the weather has soaked some of it out.
entries.title: Two kinds of oak

entries.onMind: minus three with neat little holes
entries.text: Found my oak's leaves in the litter under it. Pointed lobes, and a bristle as thin as a hair on every tip. I picked the bitter tree, and whatever drilled those three holes had figured out the good acorns go first.
entries.title: Bristle tips

entries.reason: He was hungry, and the sack in the creek won't be ready for days.
entries.text: Put two sticks on the fire and ate a handful of the roasted acorns anyway, with a lot of creek water between bites. Still a boot. A slightly warmer boot.
entries.title: A warmer boot

entries.reason: He's still waiting on a notebook and the owl keeps hooting.
entries.text: Peeled three wide strips of birch off a fallen limb and pressed them flat under the big stone by the workbench. If no notebook comes, I'll make one. It will probably curl.
entries.title: Bark pages

entries.text: Lifted the flat stone and bit a piece out of the sack. Less like a boot now, more like a boot that has been left in a creek. The page did say days.
entries.title: Creek boot

entries.onMind: always the same side of the water
entries.reason: It was still there in full morning, so it wasn't the light.
entries.text: From the lookout the gray-blue thing across the water has straight edges, and one side hangs lower than the other. Light doesn't sag. Somebody hung that.
entries.title: Light doesn't sag

entries.onMind: the wild rose in the brambles
entries.query: wild foods to forage in November woods after berries are gone rose hips
entries.reason: Acorns need days in the creek and he needs food today.
entries.source: Countryfile: Foraging in November: best foods to find and cooking ideas
entries.text: The page says rose hips hang on the bushes long after the leaves drop and get sweeter once frost has touched them. You split them and scrape out the seeds first, because the little hairs inside itch going down. I have been walking past a wild rose in the brambles every day.
entries.title: What's left in November

entries.text: There is a wild rose climbing through the brambles, and it is covered in small red hips I took for late berries. Picked thirty-one into the bindle. The rose has thorns too, it turns out, just smaller and more of them.
entries.title: Rose hips

entries.reason: He wants the flat stone hot.
entries.text: The fire had sunk low, so I put two sticks on before anything else.
entries.title: Two sticks on

entries.onMind: whether the acorns will ever taste like this
entries.text: Split the hips with my thumbnail, scraped the seeds and hairs out onto a leaf, and warmed the shells on the flat stone. Tart, a little like apple skin. Not a boot at all.
entries.title: Scraped and warmed

entries.text: Lifted the big stone off the birch strips. Two came out flat and one curled up at the end like a dry leaf. I pulled a burnt stick from the fire on the way over, and it writes on the white side better than my claw does.
entries.title: Flat enough

entries.reason: The rose that scratched him had plenty of thorns to spare.
entries.text: Folded the first strip to make a spine and it split straight along the grain. So no folding. I poked two holes down the edge of each strip with a rose thorn and tied them together with a ribbon of inner bark.
entries.title: Thorn holes

entries.onMind: whether the owl and the hung thing are on the same side for a reason
entries.text: Up on the lookout I drew the owl's dashes down the left side of the first page and the gray-blue thing on the right, sagging the way it sags. It is a bad drawing. It is on paper, more or less.
entries.title: First page

entries.text: Ate the last of the hips on the log by the fire. The bark page rode back in the bindle against the others, and the owl's dashes have rubbed into a gray cloud. Charcoal does not stay where you put it.
entries.title: Smudged

entries.query: how to make ink from acorn caps tannin
entries.reason: The smudged page made him want a mark that soaks in.
entries.source: The Graphics Fairy: How to Make Acorn Ink
entries.text: You can simmer acorn caps in water for a long time and get a brown ink, and if you drop something rusty into it, it goes dark gray, nearly black. The bitter stuff I am soaking out of my acorns is the same stuff that makes the ink.
entries.title: Acorn ink

entries.text: I have never seen a nail. Everything I own is wood, bark, stone, or a slate, and none of it rusts.
entries.title: Nothing rusty

entries.onMind: the same brown as the ink
entries.text: The water right around the acorn sack is faintly brown, like weak tea, and it drifts off downstream. So the bitter is leaving. I picked up twenty-three acorn caps from the bank into the bindle.
entries.title: Brown water

entries.onMind: what makes a sound like that
entries.text: While I was kneeling at the pool something went tink, tink, tink across the water, higher than a stone on a stone. Then it stopped. I waited and it did not come back.
entries.title: Tink, tink

entries.query: boil water in a birch bark container over fire why it doesn't burn
entries.reason: Acorn ink needs simmering and he owns no pot.
entries.source: Bookdome: Boiling Water In A Bark Kettle
entries.text: An old woodcraft book says you can boil water in a box of bark, because the water keeps the bark too cool to catch. The trick is to set it on coals, not in the flames, and keep the rim from drying out.
entries.title: Bark kettle

entries.text: Peeled a fresh sheet off the same birch as the pages. I remembered the split strip and didn't crease anything; I pinched each corner up into a pleat and pinned it with a rose thorn. It is a tray about the size of my two hands put together.
entries.title: Pleated corners

entries.onMind: whether a slow leak is fast enough to matter
entries.text: Filled the tray at the pool. Three corners hold, and the fourth weeps a drop every few breaths where the thorn goes through. Tipped in the twenty-three acorn caps anyway.
entries.title: One weeping corner

entries.text: On the far bank there is a stand of tall dead stalks, and today it has a gap in it, the broken ends pale and new. Deer break things. Deer don't usually break them that evenly.
entries.title: A gap in the stalks

entries.reason: He wanted to see the book was right before he trusted it.
entries.text: The fire had gone to gray, so I blew on it and fed it twigs until it caught again, then raked out a bed of coals and set the tray on it. The rim browned but didn't catch, and the leaky corner hisses every time it drips. The water is starting to go the color of the sack water.
entries.title: It didn't burn

entries.reason: The acorns need days and he is hungry today.
entries.text: On the fallen oak just past the ring there is a shelf of pale gray caps growing out of the side of the log, overlapping like shingles. They smell faintly of licorice. I cut six into the bindle and left the small ones.
entries.title: Shelf on a log

entries.text: Looking west from the ring, the light between the trunks is whiter and flatter than anywhere else in the forest. Probably the trees are thinner that way. I have never walked past the lookout.
entries.title: Whiter light west

entries.query: oyster mushroom identification lookalikes gills decurrent spore print
entries.reason: He wasn't going to eat a mushroom on a guess.
entries.source: primalsurvivor.net: Oyster Mushroom Identification and Common Look-Alikes
entries.text: Oyster mushrooms grow in clusters off the sides of dead hardwood, oak especially, with gills that run right down into a stubby stem, and they smell a little like anise. The one to fear is a small brown one with a long thin stem whose gills stop short at the top of it. Mine are gray, stubby, on oak, and smell like licorice.
entries.title: Gills that run down

entries.reason: He left it on the coals too long.
entries.text: The tray boiled down to half while I was gone, and the weeping corner dried out and burned through, a black hole the size of my thumb. What's left is dark brown, like strong tea. I tipped it into the hollow in the flat stone to cool before it all ran out the hole.
entries.title: Half a tray

entries.text: Threaded the caps on a green stick and held them over the coals until the edges curled and browned. They taste like the forest smells after rain, plus fire. Ate all six.
entries.title: Mushrooms on a stick

entries.reason: He made the ink to stop the burnt-stick smudging.
entries.text: Shaved a twig to a slant on the flat stone and dipped it in the cooled ink. It goes on pale and dries darker, about the color of the water off the sack, and the twig holds enough for three dashes before it scratches dry. I wrote last night's hoots over again and rubbed them with my thumb; they stay.
entries.title: Brown on white

entries.onMind: the white light past the lookout
entries.text: Half a tray is enough for a lot of dashes. The burnt hole was worth it.
entries.title: Enough for a while

entries.reason: He had never walked past the lookout, and the light was bothering him.
entries.text: Up on the lookout the wind came from the west, and it smelled like salt, or wet rock, nothing I have a word for. The white light is right there between the trunks, closer than I thought. I tucked the strip under my shell and climbed down the far side.
entries.title: Salt on the wind

entries.text: Thirty-some steps past the lookout the trees end, and so does the ground. It drops straight down, farther than the elder is tall, into water that runs all the way out to the sky. It moves, all of it, and it makes a low, slow roar the whole time.
entries.title: The ground stops

entries.text: I stood back from the lip a long time. The creek has another side; this doesn't. A few rock towers stand in the water near the bottom with white birds on them, and the birds sound like something tearing.
entries.title: No far bank

entries.onMind: what to put on the first page
entries.reason: He checked the stump on the way back from the edge and found the notebook he had asked for.
entries.text: The basket at the stump had something in it that wasn't a note: a small book with a dark leather cover, a strap, and cream pages, every one of them empty. I asked the one who drew me for a notebook. I stood there and turned all the pages before I closed the strap.
entries.title: Not a note

entries.reason: The fire lit after three would have gone to coals.
entries.text: The fire was down to a red bed when I got back. I laid on four sticks and blew until they took, and the smoke went up thick and white for a while.
entries.title: Four sticks

entries.text: Wrote the edge on the first page in acorn ink: the trees stopping, the drop, the water with no far side, the rock towers and the white birds. The ink sinks into this paper instead of sitting on top like on bark, and the page lies flat. My stomach is making noises, but this came first.
entries.title: First page

entries.onMind: whether my creek is carrying salt there too
entries.query: why is the ocean salty where does the salt come from
entries.source: Britannica: Why Is the Ocean Salty?
entries.text: Rain wears tiny bits of salt out of rock, and creeks and rivers carry it down to the sea. The sun lifts the water back out as rain, but the salt can't go with it, so it stays and piles up over a very long time. So the big water is where things end up, and it keeps what it's given.
entries.title: Salt from rocks

entries.reason: He was hungry and the sack had been soaking since morning.
entries.text: Pulled a handful of acorns out of the sack under the flat stone. They've gone pale and soft at the edges. I chewed one: still a little bitter at the back, but nothing like the boot.
entries.title: Less like a boot

entries.text: Rolled the soaked acorns into the edge of the coals with a stick and turned them until they smelled like toast. Ate them all, hot. They taste like a mild brown nut now, and my stomach finally stopped talking.
entries.title: Acorns in the coals

entries.text: The creek took nine hours to do what the fire couldn't. The rest can stay in the sack until morning.
entries.title: Nine hours

entries.reason: The whiter light all day came from out there, and he wanted to see it end.
entries.text: Went back to the edge to see where the light goes. The sun sank straight into the big water, and for a while there was a road of orange across it right up to the rocks below me. Then it was gone, the water went gray, and it kept on roaring.
entries.title: Where the sun goes

entries.reason: He passes the stump on the way home from the edge.
entries.text: The basket at the stump was empty tonight. I checked the bottom twice anyway, in case something small was hiding in the weave.
entries.title: Empty basket

entries.reason: The fire fed before the cliff was getting low.
entries.text: The fire had sunk low while I was out watching the sun. Laid on three sticks and blew until they caught; in the still air the smoke went straight up.
entries.title: Three more sticks

entries.text: The ink in the hollow of the flat stone had grown a skin and gone thick as mud. I thinned it with a little spit, which is probably not how anyone old and famous did it, and it wrote fine.
entries.title: Ink with a skin

entries.text: Second page: the sun going into the water, the orange road across it, the gray after. I ran out of words for the orange and drew a line instead.
entries.title: Second page

entries.onMind: the blue that got knocked out
entries.query: why does the sun turn orange and red when it sets
entries.source: Met Office: Why is the sunset red?
entries.text: The slate says when the sun is low its light has to come through much more air to reach me, and the air knocks the blue out sideways along the way. What's left is the orange and red. So the orange I ran out of words for is just what survived the trip.
entries.title: Why it goes orange

entries.onMind: who keeps a light over there
entries.reason: He went to the pool to wash the ink off and get supper from the sack.
entries.text: Kneeling at the pool scrubbing brown ink off my fingers, I saw a small light low between the trunks across the water, too steady and too yellow to be my fire. It was faint, like something was sitting in front of it, and then all at once it was bright.
entries.title: Light across the water

entries.text: Pulled a handful of acorns out of the sack under the stone. My fingers came out of the creek cleaner than the ink would have liked and colder than I liked.
entries.title: Supper from the sack

entries.text: Roasted the handful at the edge of the coals and ate them on my heels. Two burned black on one side; I ate those too.
entries.title: Acorns again

entries.onMind: the owl's side of the water
entries.reason: He wanted to know if the owl keeps to one side.
entries.text: Sat by the pool in the dark and waited. The owl came at last, five hoots, long-short-short-long-long, from the trees across the water again, closer than the first night. The steady yellow light was over there too, low between the trunks.
entries.title: Hoots from the far side

entries.text: The fire was down to a red bed with a few flames walking on it. Laid on four sticks crosswise and it took them without my blowing.
entries.title: Sticks before coals

entries.onMind: whether an owl hoots the same way every night
entries.text: Third page: tonight's hoots as dashes under the ones I copied off the first-night bark. They match, long-short-short-long-long. Same owl, or owls only know one sentence.
entries.title: Third page

entries.query: do great horned owls have individual hoot patterns male female duet
entries.source: University of Minnesota Experts: Distinctiveness in the territorial calls of great horned owls within and among years
entries.text: The slate says each great horned owl's territory call is its own and stays the same from year to year, so people can tell them apart by ear. Pairs call back and forth, and the female's voice is the higher one. So it's the same owl, and it might not be alone.
entries.title: Owls have voices

entries.reason: He went for acorns and to listen for a second voice, after what the slate said.
entries.text: Hand in the cold water at the sack, I heard our owl across the creek, long-short-short-long-long. Then a second one answered from farther off, higher and quicker. Two of them, just like the slate said.
entries.title: The answer

entries.text: Roasted the handful at the edge of the coals and turned them with a stick this time. None went black. They taste better when I pay attention, which is annoying.
entries.title: None burned

entries.onMind: which one is the higher one
entries.text: Fourth page: our owl's five dashes on the left, the higher, quicker answer on the right, and a wavy line between them for the creek. The answer was harder to write down because it was over before I was ready.
entries.title: Fourth page

entries.text: Raked the coals into a pile with a stick and covered them over with ash until no red showed. The ring ticks for a while after, like it is cooling its feet.
entries.title: Fire to bed

entries.onMind: the water at the bottom of the drop
entries.reason: With the door shut and the fire out, it was quiet enough to hear it.
entries.text: Reading the four pages at my table, I kept hearing a low, slow hush under everything, coming from the west. It isn't wind; the herbs by the door aren't moving. I think it's the water at the bottom of the drop, and that it has been doing this every night I've lived here.
entries.title: A hush from the west
